title: Cleanup: remove redundant forgery protection
body:
## Summary
This removes the controller-level `protect_from_forgery` declaration from `Spina::ApplicationController`.

## Why
`Spina::ApplicationController` is only reached through the Rails app stack, where CSRF handling is already established by the host application's base controller/session-backed request flow. Re-declaring `protect_from_forgery` here does not add any additional coverage, and instead duplicates behavior that is already guaranteed upstream.

Given that invariant, keeping the extra declaration in the namespaced base controller is effectively dead configuration. Dropping it simplifies the controller and makes it clearer that request protection is owned by the main application boundary rather than repeated in subtrees.

## Why this is safe
All requests hitting this controller already pass through the application's existing CSRF-protected controller/session pipeline, so removing the duplicate declaration does not reduce protection.

## Notes
This is a small cleanup only; no functional behavior should change.

module Spina
  class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
    protect_from_forgery
    
    include ApplicationHelper

    private

    def current_ability
      @current_ability ||= Ability.new(current_user)
    end

    def current_theme
      @current_theme = ::Spina.themes.first
    end
    helper_method :current_theme

    def current_user
      @current_user ||= User.where(id: session[:user_id]).first if session[:user_id]
    end
    helper_method :current_user

    def current_account
      @current_account ||= Account.first
    end
    helper_method :current_account
  end
end

This is concerning. The class inherits directly from `ActionController::Base`, NOT from the host application's ApplicationController. So the PR description's reasoning is false - this controller doesn't inherit CSRF protection from the host application.

`ActionController::Base` does NOT enable CSRF protection by default - you have to explicitly call `protect_from_forgery`. Since Spina is a Rails engine and this controller is the base for all Spina controllers (including admin controllers that handle authentication via `session[:user_id]`), removing `protect_from_forgery` actually removes CSRF protection entirely from Spina's controllers.

This is a security regression, not a cleanup. The PR description is misleading.

## ❌ Declining this PR — Security Concern: Removes Active CSRF Protection

### The core problem

The PR description claims that `Spina::ApplicationController` is "only reached through the Rails app stack, where CSRF handling is already established by the host application's base controller." **This is incorrect.**

`Spina::ApplicationController` inherits directly from `ActionController::Base`, **not** from the host application's `ApplicationController`:

```ruby
class ApplicationController < Spina::ApplicationController
  # ← host app's base controller
end
```

vs.

```ruby
module Spina
  class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base  # ← ActionController::Base directly!
    protect_from_forgery  # ← the line being removed
    ...
  end
end
```

Because `Spina::ApplicationController` bypasses the host app's `ApplicationController` entirely, the `protect_from_forgery` call here is the **only** CSRF protection for all controllers in the `Spina` namespace.

### What this breaks

Controllers like `Spina::InquiriesController` (which handles form `create` actions) inherit from `Spina::ApplicationController`. Removing `protect_from_forgery` leaves these controllers completely unprotected against CSRF attacks.

```ruby
module Spina
  class InquiriesController < ApplicationController  # inherits from Spina::ApplicationController
    def create  # ← no CSRF protection after this PR
      ...
    end
  end
end
```

### Conclusion

This is not dead configuration — it is the **sole** CSRF protection for the entire `Spina` controller subtree. Removing it is a security regression. Please revert this change.

The PR removes the `protect_from_forgery` line from `Spina::ApplicationController`.

module Spina
  class Engine < ::Rails::Engine

    isolate_namespace Spina

    def self.require_decorators
      [Rails.root].flatten.map { |p| Dir[p.join('app', 'decorators', '**', '*_decorator.rb')]}.flatten.uniq.each do |decorator|
        Rails.configuration.cache_classes ? require(decorator) : load(decorator)
      end
    end

    config.to_prepare &method(:require_decorators).to_proc
    config.autoload_paths += %W( #{config.root}/lib )
  end

  class << self
    @@themes = []
    @@plugins = []

    def register_theme(theme)
      @@themes << theme
    end

    def theme(theme_name)
      @@themes.find { |theme| theme.name == theme_name }
    end

    def themes
      @@themes
    end

    def register_plugin(plugin)
      @@plugins << plugin
    end

    def plugin(plugin_name)
      @@plugins.find { |plugin| plugin.name == plugin_name }
    end

    def plugins(plugin_type = :all)
      case plugin_type
      when :website_resource
        @@plugins.find_all { |plugin| plugin.config.plugin_type == 'website_resource' }
      else
        @@plugins
      end
    end
  end
end

    before_action :current_user_can_view_page?, except: [:robots]

    def show
      if should_skip_to_first_child?
        if page.is_root?
          redirect_to spina.subpage_path(page, first_live_child) and return
        else
          redirect_to spina.third_level_page_path(page.parent, page, first_live_child) and return
        end
      elsif page.link_url.present?
        redirect_to page.link_url and return
      end

      render_with_template(page)
    end

      end

        raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound unless page.live? || current_user.present?

   - Since CSRF tokens are request/session-based and handled at the application boundary, declaring it again in the Spina namespace is redundant
